     "subtitle": "From the Department of Economics to the calling of a childbirth educator: The joy of motherhood versus trauma",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains how her personal experience prompted her to research pregnancy and childbirth.",
     "content": "In the new episode of the podcast, host **Željka Markić** welcomed **Andrea Piškor**, a certified childbirth educator and birth companion, and mother of three boys and one girl. Although she holds a Master's degree in Economics by profession and is a former school teacher, her life path completely changed after her own experience of motherhood, especially after a difficult first childbirth. Today, she owns a tutoring business through which she individually prepares pregnant women and their spouses for pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and breastfeeding. The host points out that she learned about her work through a close friend to whom Andrea provided invaluable support and preparation of a kind they did not expect in our environment.\n\nSpeaking about the transition from economics to the field of childbirth education, Andrea Piškor explains how it all started fifteen years ago, after her first childbirth. For a full ten years, she researched this topic in her free time, looking for answers to the question of whether childbirth really has to look the way she experienced it. As she matured spiritually and grew in faith, she began to wonder if God's plan for motherhood was for a woman to emerge from childbirth physically and emotionally wounded, hurt at the level of spirit, soul, and body, feeling discouraged, sad, and abandoned.\n\nA particular restlessness was provoked in her by a common social phrase that felt like a slap in the face to her: *\"Everything is fine as long as you and the baby are alive.\"* Željka Markić follows up by pointing out that this minimum must by no means be the maximum, because mothers deserve fullness, pride, and fulfillment in what they have achieved. The guest agrees and emphasizes that every childbirth—even the fastest and easiest one—is extremely exhausting for the female organism, but despite this, at its core there must be an indescribable joy that must not be taken away from the woman.\n\nThis joy is not just an abstract concept, but is also scientifically proven. Piškor explains that childbirth is initiated and guided by **oxytocin**, known as the hormone of love and joy. It is secreted in very intimate situations, when a woman feels safe, supported, and encouraged. Through years of working in her profession, and after her second childbirth and third pregnancy, Andrea definitely decided to leave her previous job and dedicate herself completely to what she feels is her true calling—bringing the message to all families that childbirth is not torment and that motherhood should be joyful.",

     "subtitle": "A slap from the system and entering postpartum 'from a deficit'",
     "screenshot_description": "The guest talks about being unprepared for her first childbirth and the clash with reality in the maternity ward.",
     "content": "When asked by the host what exactly made her first childbirth so difficult, Andrea Piškor makes an important distinction between a medically difficult childbirth and a traumatic experience. The same course of childbirth can be quite acceptable for one woman, while for another it can cause deep trauma, which is why someone else's experience must never be minimized. Her first childbirth was indeed medically demanding, prolonged, and complicated due to the specific position of the baby, but what left the greatest trauma was her own unpreparedness.\n\nAs a first-time mother, she arrived at the maternity ward completely unprepared for the reality of the system. Her only preparation was reading the book *Duhovni pristup rađanju* (Spiritual Approach to Childbirth), because of which she naively expected the conditions described by the author in the book. She consciously avoided listening to other people's negative experiences—which women with difficult childbirths often feel the need to recount—and went to the hospital full of trust, expecting joy, tenderness, and respect.\n\nInstead, she was met by, as she puts it, a \"slap from the system\". Due to the huge crowd in the maternity ward and the chronic shortage of medical staff, general chaos reigned. The combination of a difficult childbirth and such an environment resulted in her feeling extremely bad, entering the entire postpartum period \"from a deficit\". It is precisely this painful experience that has enabled her today to deeply understand the women she works with and to realize how crucial a positive childbirth experience is for everything that follows after the child comes into the world.",

     "subtitle": "Comprehensive preparation program: Why don't we know the basics in an age of accessible information?",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains the four parts of her educational program and the problem of misinformation.",
     "content": "Today, Andrea Piškor provides parents with precisely what she lacked, combining two roles: that of a childbirth educator and that of a birth companion. Her **comprehensive preparation program** consists of four parts, and couples choose for themselves whether they want to go through all of them or only certain segments:\n- **Preparation for pregnancy** (what is normal to expect and how to enjoy pregnancy)\n- **Preparation for childbirth**\n- **Preparation for breastfeeding**\n- **Preparation for postpartum**\n\nParents most often opt for education on childbirth itself and breastfeeding. Piškor warns of the paradox of today's time: despite information being more accessible than ever, couples are often misinformed and do not know fundamental biological facts—at the level of elementary school science and social studies—such as what the uterus looks like or where fertilization actually takes place. Education therefore serves as the last chance to discover the beauty of God's creation in the female body and to understand all the changes that occur.\n\nWhen couples adopt this knowledge base, they can make decisions in peace at crucial moments. The guest emphasizes that in childbirth there is no absolutely good or bad decision; every decision is good if the spouses made it together and in peace. Although childbirth can never be fully planned nor will it look exactly as they imagined it, knowing the process brings much-needed security.\n\nAfter education follows the role of the birth companion. Andrea remains available to the family during pregnancy, when the first contractions start, all the way up to the first month after the baby's birth, when parents have the most questions. In doing so, she strictly watches her boundaries: she does not interfere in the parents' decisions, does not make them on their behalf, and does not negotiate with the medical staff. Her role is to provide emotional support. During the recording of the podcast itself, Piškor revealed that she is currently in contact with three women in labor—they have just welcomed one baby, are waiting for the second, and the third pregnant woman was sent home from the maternity ward and is expecting the start of labor at any moment.",

     "subtitle": "The power of maternal intuition and burdens that are rarely talked about",
     "screenshot_description": "Željka Markić and Andrea Piškor discuss the importance of maternal intuition and independent decision-making.",
     "content": "Željka Markić particularly praised her guest's working methodology because it actively involves fathers and encourages couples to make decisions independently. In doing so, the host shared a personal anecdote related to the recent birth of her grandson. Since both she and her husband are doctors and raised four children themselves, the young parents often consulted them. However, at one point she felt the need to say to her daughter-in-law: *\"Look, I know all sorts of things, I gave birth to four children, I have experience and knowledge as a doctor, but you are the mom, I am not the mom. You have gathered all the information and you do what you feel you need to do.\"*\n\nAndrea Piškor follows up on this by pointing out that she always repeats the same sentence to her couples: **maternal intuition** is called maternal for a reason—it is neither the grandmother's, nor the mother-in-law's, nor the aunt's, nor even the birth companion's intuition. When a pregnant woman is in doubt about whether to head to the maternity ward or stay at home, Andrea asks her how she feels and if she is worried. If there is worry, there is no point in forcing her to stay at home; the right time to leave is when the husband and wife agree to do so. Sometimes, just a short message of support is enough for a woman, such as *\"I am thinking of you, praying for you, everything is fine\"*.\n\nFor such support to be effective, continuity is key. Piškor advises couples to contact her at least midway through the pregnancy so they have time to build a relationship of trust. In practice, she has prepared couples not only for their first, but also for their third, fourth, fifth, and even sixth childbirth. It often happens that a woman in her fifth pregnancy feels a strong fear from the very conception due to previous traumatic experiences in the delivery room.\n\nIn addition to fear and medical diagnoses, women today also carry numerous other burdens, such as a lack of understanding from their immediate family regarding their openness to life. Because of comments from their surroundings such as *\"Why are you complaining now, whose fault is it that you're pregnant again\"*, mothers feel they have no right to complain about fatigue or a hard day. Therefore, Piškor points out, dryly listing the four stages of labor is nowhere near as important as recognizing the whole person in front of you. Pregnancy and childbirth are not exclusively medical events reduced to the mere survival of mother and child, as our system often treats them, but deeply emotional and spiritual transitions into parenthood.",

     "subtitle": "Why rush childbirth? Cultural myths and the reality of Croatian maternity wards",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains why it is important to give childbirth time and how cultural patterns affect the perception of pain.",
     "content": "Answering the question of what is the biggest obstacle to childbirth remaining a positive memory, Andrea Piškor points out the lack of awareness that childbirth is a process that takes time and needs to be given time. Society must move away from culturally inherited patterns and stories about how a woman \"suffered for two days\". The guest reminds us that nobody has the strongest contractions for a full two days and asks the question: what are twelve hours or two days in our entire life when a new life is coming into the world?\n\nInstead of rushing childbirth, couples should immerse themselves in that process. It is completely natural to spend half a day at home in mild contractions, walking, preparing lunch for the older children, and peacefully awaiting departure with one's husband. When childbirth is approached without the fear of its duration, it does not wound, but rather empowers the woman, brings the spouses closer together, and spiritually elevates the marriage to a completely new level.\n\nOn the other hand, balancing such an approach with the reality of the Croatian healthcare system represents a major challenge. Piškor describes the system as sluggish and flawed, but emphasizes that positive changes are nevertheless coming, and primarily from the women in labor themselves. In doing so, she shows great understanding for the medical staff, who are chronically overextended. Midwives literally run through their entire shift, which is why it is unrealistic to expect that in such conditions they can continuously stand by one woman in labor and take care of her psychological state.\n\nIn well-organized systems, which already exist in neighboring countries across the border, a pregnant woman meets her midwife during pregnancy and goes through everything that is important to her and her husband with her. In Croatia, however, a woman arrives at the maternity ward not knowing who is on shift. During recent renovations of maternity wards, it even happened that due to overbooking, women in labor were turned away at the door and redirected to another hospital because it was assessed that they were not yet in an advanced stage of labor. In such circumstances—when a woman has to change hospitals or when a doctor immediately proceeds to a vaginal examination without introducing himself—the body experiences stress, the feeling of safety disappears, and the secretion of oxytocin is blocked.",

     "subtitle": "The role of the father in the delivery room and the importance of informed consent",
     "screenshot_description": "The host and guest discuss informed consent using the example of epidural anesthesia.",
     "content": "Precisely because of the lack of continuous midwifery care in Croatian hospitals, the role of the birth companion gains importance. However, Andrea Piškor reveals that she very rarely physically goes with women to the maternity ward. The main reason lies in her firm stance that the primary support for a woman in childbirth should be her husband. When pregnant women ask her if she would go with them to the birth, she always suggests that they first go through the education together with their husband. \n\nMen often carry too great a burden and expectation that they have to do something \"excessively important and smart\" in the delivery room, so out of insecurity they prefer to yield their place to the birth companion. However, when they realize during the education that it is enough for the woman just that they are physically present with her, a huge burden falls from them and the vast majority of husbands decide to be with their wife. If a choice must be made between the birth companion and the child's father, the father must always have priority, because presence at the birth blesses and empowers the whole family. Although in the past it was considered that a man's place is not in the delivery room, but in a café while waiting for news, Piškor notes with satisfaction that in the last fifteen years Croatian society has strongly moved away from such thinking.\n\nŽeljka Markić then referred to the practice in neighboring countries where pregnant women have a mandatory half-hour meeting with an anesthesiologist before childbirth. Such a conversation, the host points out, saves the healthcare system both time and money, and brings the woman peace and what is called **informed consent**. As an example, she cited a doctor who explained in detail to a first-time mother all the options related to epidural anesthesia, including the possibility of changing her mind during the birth itself. However, he also gave her professional advice: if she plans to have more children, it is smarter to go through the first childbirth without an epidural so that her body \"learns childbirth\" and retains a natural connection with the process, while with the second or third child, when the body already knows the mechanism of giving birth, she can freely take anesthesia.\n\nAndrea Piškor follows up with the information that in even better-organized systems, midwives independently manage the entire normal pregnancy, and even make home visits to the family, while gynecologists are reserved exclusively for high-risk pregnancies. Since a birth companion is not in the medical profession, she encourages pregnant women to take responsibility and ask all medical questions directly to their gynecologists in the office, instead of looking for answers on internet forums and social networks after the examination.",

     "subtitle": "Birth plan and the cascade of routine interventions: The case of episiotomy",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains why the medical interventions themselves are not the problem for women, but the lack of communication.",
     "content": "One of the tools for preparing for the maternity ward is the **birth plan**. Piškor likes to simplify this concept, which men especially appreciate: a birth plan does not necessarily have to be a written document, but a mutual agreement between husband and wife after they have become acquainted with the physiology of natural childbirth and the real conditions in Croatian maternity wards. Over coffee, the couple talks about how big the gap is between their wishes and hospital possibilities, and defines what is truly important to them.\n\nWhen it comes to medical interventions, the guest takes a very realistic stance: every intervention is useful if the benefit it brings is greater than the current state in which the woman in labor finds herself. The problem arises when interventions are performed **routinely**, without medical justification, which often triggers a whole cascade of new procedures. Nevertheless, practice shows that the greatest trauma for women is not caused by the intervention itself—not even an **episiotomy** (cutting the perineum), which all pregnant women fear—but by the way in which it is performed. When a doctor explains why he proposes a procedure and includes the woman in the decision, she can retain a positive childbirth experience even with an episiotomy. Traumas occur when procedures, such as breaking the water, are done without any announcement or explanation, so the woman only realizes afterwards what was done to her.\n\nŽeljka Markić presented statistical data according to which **France** has the lowest rate of episiotomies (around 8 percent), while Croatia, together with **Germany** and **Austria**, hovers around 20 percent. Since these are anatomically the same women and the same difficulty of childbirth, the host concludes that the low rate in France is the result of a clear decision by the profession, which assessed that the severe consequences that episiotomy is supposedly meant to prevent are in reality much rarer.\n\nAndrea Piškor confirms that numerous studies show that routine episiotomy has no real benefit, but warns that in Croatia the practice is not uniform at the system level, depending instead exclusively on the individual—the doctor who happens to be on duty. As an extreme example, she cited the case of a woman who came for her fourth childbirth, after having previously given birth to twins vaginally, and a routine episiotomy was performed on her before she had practically even reached the table. The consequences of such unnecessary procedures are difficult movement, painful recovery, and problems with establishing breastfeeding. \n\nDespite the criticisms, both interlocutors conclude that the job of gynecologists and midwives is one of the most stressful specializations. The head of the delivery room must have top-notch managerial skills because he never knows whether the bell at the entrance will ring three, thirteen, or thirty-three times during his shift. Doctors do what they were trained for—they save lives and preserve health—while comprehensive emotional and spiritual care for a woman in labor requires mutual cooperation and understanding between the medical staff, birth companions, and the family itself.",

     "subtitle": "Childbirth is just the beginning: How the experience of giving birth shapes postpartum and cooperation with the healthcare system",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains how a positive childbirth experience reduces the risk of postpartum depression.",
     "content": "Childbirth educator **Andrea Piškor** emphasizes that there is often a misconception in society that the whole story ends with the act of childbirth itself, while it is actually just the beginning. A positive childbirth experience, in which the mother was respected and from which she emerges emotionally and physically stable, drastically reduces the risk of developing postpartum depression and other depressive states. With the support of her husband, a birth companion, or a close person, a woman recovers much faster, thereby preventing a situation in which a traumatic childbirth literally \"steals\" the joy of early motherhood from the mother.\n\nHost **Željka Markić** praised the realistic approach of her guest, who does not deny the shortcomings of the healthcare system, but encourages parents to get the maximum out of the existing frameworks through education and preparation. Piškor points out that women in labor need doctors and delivery rooms, but also points to absurdities in practice. For example, she describes the lying-down position for giving birth as the hardest and ugliest for a woman, reminding us that ever since 1999, a document of the **World Health Organization** has recommended that a woman in labor be encouraged to be active and move during contractions, rather than lie down. Although doctors and midwives themselves are often aware that a different approach would be better, they are limited by the conditions in which they work, which is why cooperation with birth companions is necessary in order to encompass the woman holistically—in spirit, soul, and body.\n\nAs a concrete example of unused potential in hospitals, Markić cites a case in which a maternity ward possesses a tub with warm water, which is proven to make enduring contractions easier and reduces the need for an episiotomy, yet the medical staff does not offer women the possibility of using it at all. Piškor adds that staff who literally run through their entire shift cannot be blamed for avoiding additional procedures in already complicated conditions. On the other hand, although Croatian maternity wards organize \"Open Days\" and workshops, this often boils down to a mere tour of the premises. When the pregnant woman finally comes to give birth, she is met by a different shift and a different doctor, so the rules she heard at the course no longer apply, because much in the Croatian system still depends on the momentary decision of an individual, rather than a uniform protocol.",

     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor recounts an anecdote about a pregnant woman who returned to her apartment from the garage because she felt she was about to give birth.",
     "content": "Although she always repeats to her clients that childbirth is a marathon, not a sprint, and that it needs to be given time, **Andrea Piškor** reveals that in her practice, real \"movie-like scenarios\" of fast, unplanned births outside the hospital happen several times a year. She admits that, judging exclusively by her own childbirths, she herself would have thought such stories were fabrications, but her experience working with pregnant women has shown her the opposite.\n\nShe shared an anecdote about a married couple who set off for the maternity ward in the winter. When they went down to the garage, the pregnant woman realized that the birth had progressed so much that they would not make it to the hospital, and she resolutely told her husband: *\"I do not want to give birth in the garage, I want to go back upstairs because it is winter and I am going to give birth now.\"* They barely managed to get back to the warm apartment, the husband called an ambulance, and the baby was born at home. Host **Željka Markić** noticed how good preparation came to the fore even in that crisis situation, because the woman listened to her body and made a sensible decision not to give birth in a cold and dirty space.\n\nOther cases involve women who have given birth before and already know contractions well, but are completely surprised by the speed of the process. Piškor describes a situation in which a pregnant woman contacted her with mild symptoms, thinking she might give birth only \"in the coming days\", only to contact her again just fifteen minutes later with the news that she had just given birth in her own bathroom while going to the toilet and that they were now waiting for an ambulance. In such moments, the guest points out, it is crucial that both parents are calm and secure in each other because they know the physiology of the process itself.",

     "subtitle": "The economics of breastfeeding: The law of supply and demand and debunking myths about 'weak milk'",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains how breastfeeding works according to the economic law of supply and demand.",
     "content": "Preparation for the period after childbirth largely includes education about breastfeeding while still pregnant. Although breastfeeding is the most natural way of feeding because humans are mammals, **Andrea Piškor** emphasizes that it is at the same time a skill that is learned and perfected. Many mothers today enter this process with a great lack of experience because they belong to generations that, while growing up, did not have the opportunity to see other women breastfeeding, since until recently it was suppressed from the public space.\n\nThe guest sharply rejects culturally inherited stereotypes and prejudices that women encounter, sometimes even in the maternity wards themselves—such as comments that the mother has \"breasts that are too small\", that she immediately needs nipple shields, or that her \"milk is weak\". Starting from the perspective of faith and biology, Piškor asks a logical question: how is it possible that God would create man perfectly, and yet a mother's body cannot create sufficiently good milk, because of which the human species would have died out long ago? Except in about 10 percent of cases where real medical diagnoses and pathologies exist, every healthy mother can breastfeed her child.\n\nWith a Master's degree in Economics, Piškor vividly explains the process of lactation through the **law of supply and demand**:\n- **Active stimulation instead of waiting:** Mothers often contact her on the third day after a Cesarean section saying that they are \"waiting for their milk to come in\". Piškor warns that merely waiting or drinking the most expensive nursing teas will not start the process. Milk is created exclusively when the baby is at the breast and nursing, because only then does the mother's brain receive the signal to enter the lactation process.\n- **Non-nutritive sucking:** Parents must understand that in the first year of life, and especially in the first month, up to 50 percent of breastfeeding is not related to hunger. A baby has an innate instinct for sucking that provides comfort, peace, and security. Therefore, frequently asking for the breast is not a sign that the milk is \"weak\", but the child's need for the mother's closeness.\n- **Physiological breast engorgement:** Between the third and fifth day after childbirth, in 90 percent of women, the breasts suddenly become full, warm, and hard. When a mother is educated in advance, she neither panics nor ignores the condition (which could lead to mastitis), but calmly applies the learned steps and continues to enjoy the first weeks with her child.",

     "subtitle": "Vulnerability in postpartum: Why even the best intention can sound like criticism",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor talks about the sensitivity of the mother after childbirth and how those around her should approach her.",
     "content": "The period immediately after childbirth is extremely turbulent and demanding for the whole family, and knowing what follows brings much-needed peace. **Željka Markić** cites the example of a child's crying: when someone warns parents in advance that a baby's crying is naturally exhausting to listen to regardless of all the love for the child, parents cope more easily with that frustration because they know there is nothing strange about them. **Andrea Piškor** agrees, pointing out how important it is for a mother's mental health in the postpartum period to know that difficult situations happen to everyone, it is just that they are talked about too little in society.\n\nSpecial emphasis is placed on the immense emotional vulnerability of a woman after childbirth. During that period, a mother automatically translates every piece of information, advice, or even the most well-intentioned criticism from her surroundings into her own insecurity through the thought: *\"I am not a good enough mom, I am not doing this well.\"* \n\nPiškor therefore appeals to the surroundings, family, and visitors to be extremely gentle and careful. Often people come for a visit and casually toss out comments in passing like: *\"Why haven't you covered him?\", \"He is hot\"* or *\"It is a bit too warm in your apartment\"*, and then leave, leaving the mother in a complete \"system breakdown\". After such a casual remark, a woman will replay the thought a hundred times in her head of how they could have heated the apartment so much and what kind of parents they are. Instead of handing out lessons, a new mother should be approached with a lot of tact, first listening to what she has to say, and thinking five times about how to offer her any suggestion so as to preserve her self-confidence and maternal intuition.",

     "subtitle": "Concluding message to pregnant women: 'Fear is afraid of love, and childbirth is at its core joy'",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor sends a final encouraging message to all pregnant women about the beauty of childbirth.",
     "content": "When asked by host **Željka Markić** what single most important thing every pregnant woman should learn in time, **Andrea Piškor** answers that it is crucial to become aware that childbirth is a natural, physiological process that happens every day all over the world and that at its core it is—joy.\n\n*\"Fear is afraid of love. What are you afraid of? God's plan for motherhood is not fear\"*, says Piškor, reminding us that every childbirth begins with excitement and joy because parents know that their baby is finally arriving. Instead of an approach in which one just waits for everything to pass as quickly as possible with a fear of prolonged suffering, childbirth should be given importance, provided with the time and space it deserves, and acknowledged for its beauty. Intense contractions only last right before the very end of labor anyway, so one should go through the entire process with the joy of anticipating new life.\n\nAt the very end of the conversation, Piškor revealed that she operates through her website and profiles on Instagram and Facebook under the name **Blažena ti** (Support for parents in early parenthood), but pointed out that the largest number of couples and pregnant women actually come to her through word-of-mouth recommendations, which is the result of deep relationships of trust that remain long after the childbirth itself.",
